segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, good news for parents of children with asthma, dyslexia in a digital world, the media and cancer reporting, and a caution for people with high blood pressure. Don't ignore the bottom number of your pressure, what's called your diastolic.
Last November on the Health Report, we covered a study called the SPRINT trial,
which found that for people at high risk of a heart attack or stroke,
going on to high blood pressure treatment,
which aimed for a top number or systolic blood pressure of 120 or less,
was associated with significant benefits compared to the usual target of 140.
This has made many countries wonder whether they should tell doctors
to lower blood pressure targets in their patients at high risk of heart disease.
But you'll notice I've only talked about the top number, the systolic pressure,
which is the pressure generated by the heart beating and pumping blood through your arteries.
The bottom number, the diastolic pressure, is the background pressure between heartbeats
and has a critical role in keeping blood going to organs like the brain and heart.
A group led by researchers at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore was concerned that
there might be a risk in people whose diastolic pressure falls too far with more aggressive blood
pressure treatment. It's a story consumers need to know about. Bill McAvoy was the lead author,
and I spoke to him earlier today.
Patients who have very stiff blood vessels,
which is a risk factor for heart disease and stroke,
the diastolic pressure, which is the pressure, as you said,
between heartbeats tends to be lower.
And that means that there can be less perfusion of the organ
during diastole, which is, for all intents and purposes,
approximately half of the heartbeat.
And just to capture what you said there,
essentially is a low diastolic blood pressure
could be a reflection of very stiff arteries
in somebody who's already considerably at risk.
Yes. And to add to that, those patients with stiff arteries tend to have higher systolic blood pressures.
And that means that the pulse pressure, which is the difference between the two, systolic minus diastolic, is larger.
So those patients with a higher pulse pressure, which is a higher systolic and a lower diastolic, likely due to stiff arteries,
if they're going to be treated to this target of 120, they may end up with a non-treatment diastolic blood pressure that's lower than we would like.
and that has theoretical reasons for concern specifically with respect to the coronary blood flow.
The coronary arteries, as you know, are the arteries that supply the heart muscle itself.
And those coronary arteries, because they go through the heart muscle,
when the heart squeezes in systole, which is the time when the heart's pumping blood out,
those vessels are constricted and there's no flow.
So the only time that there's actually flow to the heart muscle through those coronary arteries
is during diastole.
And for that particular reason,
it could be that in diastole,
when the diastolic blood pressure is too low,
that you're getting actually reduced blood flow
to the heart muscle, which can cause damage.
So you studied 11,500 people, average age 57,
both men and women,
to look at the relationship between whether or not
you could measure heart damage by a chemical called troponin
related to their diastolic blood pressure.
Were those people being treated for their blood pressure
or this was their natural diastolic blood pressure?
It was a mix.
This was a fairly healthy population in their 50s
and specifically did not have a prior history of coronary artery disease.
So most of the patients were not on treatment.
We found that even when we stratified the analysis
based on hypertension treatment status,
that is, we looked both at the group of patients or adults
in the study who were getting treatment for blood pressure
and we looked at the group who were not on any treatment,
we saw that the results were the same.
That is, that the diastolic blood pressure,
the lower that blood pressure was,
the more likely that we saw an association with heart damage by this troponin.
And what's the significance of that raised troponin?
I mean, was it high enough to be registrable as a heart attack,
or is it just chronic damage that could lead to heart failure, for example?
More of the latter than the former.
We know from prior studies that individuals with troponin levels this high
are far more likely to have adverse outcomes, specifically adverse coronary heart disease,
cardiac death, and most particularly adverse heart failure outcomes.
So I see this as individuals who are ambulating, walking around their communities,
likely mostly asymptomatic, who had detectable levels of heart muscle injury,
relating to the lower diastolic blood pressure and the consequent reduction in the coronary blood flow.
And again, our take-home message is that the SPRINT study is important.
There are individuals who will benefit from a lower societal blood pressure.
I think that can't be underestimated.
But our real simple point in this analysis was that physicians really need to look at both.
And your cut-off that you thought was the one that was significant was 70,
that the bottom number shouldn't fall below 70?
Yeah, we certainly saw a trend for certain outcomes for heart disease
and for the trachonin outcome.
we saw a significantly elevated association in the individuals who have
vasocytic blood pressure less than 70, and particularly less than 60, would be of concern.
So what's a general practitioner to do? Because you can't treat diastolic by itself,
you've only got one blood pressure pill or one lifestyle measure. What are you to do?
I think in an individual who, for instance, has an elevated vasocytic blood pressure and
whom the general practitioner is considering blood pressure treatment, I think they need to
assess what the systolic blood pressure is. I understand that, particularly for patients who
have known coronary artery disease, have had prior bypass surgery, prior heart attacks,
that particularly in those individuals who have that history, who have a wide pulse pressure,
I think there needs to be some caution in pushing the systolic blood pressure too low.
But the SPRINT people would say, well, we did a randomized control trial and we properly studied
it in a randomized way. All you've done is looked at a group of people which is not as good evidence.
So they haven't reported the outcomes based on diastolic blood pressure.
So I would say that that's an average result.
And therefore, it's fair to say that on average, if you take a given patient and take them
at random and you treat them, if they have the criteria for sprints to a systolic of
120, they're likely going to benefit.
But for the individual who has a low diastolic blood pressure, I would advocate that those
patients not be treated as aggressively, particularly if they have a history of coronary
artery disease.
I think this is just something that puts a little bit more emphasis on the individual
rather than on the average.
It doesn't contradict the sprint study in any way.
It just really highlights the point that diastolic blood pressure shouldn't be ignored
and that for individuals who start off with that low diastolic blood pressure,
there needs to be some caution of dropping it lower,
particularly if they have known coronary artery disease.
Bill McAvoy, thanks for joining us on The Health Report.
Thank you.
Bill McAvoy is in the cardiology department at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore.
And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
25 or 30 years ago, Australia had the dubious record of having just about the highest death rates from asthma in the world.
No one knew quite why, but it was thought in part because people were overusing their reliever inhalers,
medications like Ventolin, and not using their preventers, which are usually inhaled steroids,
which actually treat the underlying disease.
Ventolin is a short-acting member of a family of medications called beta agonists,
which allow the airways to relax.
In the last few years, drug companies have produced long-acting beta agonists,
which only need to be taken once or twice a day.
It's known that these LABAs, these long-acting drugs, should not be used by themselves,
but in combination with inhaled steroids, they've conquered the market for asthma medications.
Yet no one has been absolutely sure they're safe, even in combination.
But last week, a large trial in children was published trying to answer that question,
and it follows a similar study in adults.
Someone with a close interest in this is Professor Christine Jenkins,
who's head of respiratory trials at the George Institute in Sydney.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Thank you, Norman.
So what did this study in children find?
This study is, as you said, a very large study.
In fact, it was designed to look at the safety of long-acting beta agonists
in combination with inhaled corticosteroids.
So the long-acting antagonist is not being given alone here.
It's being given in a single inhaler with an anti-inflammatory medication
versus that anti-inflammatory medication alone.
And this was a six-month study in children aged between 4 and 11.
And they looked at what we call the severe asthma-related events.
And those events were either episodes where children had attacks
so that they needed to take an oral porticosteroid, of course, of prednisone,
or even worse, might have been admitted to hospital, for instance.
And a severe asthma event, of course, also includes a death from asthma.
But most importantly, there were no deaths from asthma in this study.
And in fact, there was a very, very low rate, less than 2%, fewer than 2% of the children
actually had severe asthma-related events over this six-month period.

And what it showed was there was no difference in these outcomes between the children who took the inhaled steroid only, that is the anti-inflammatory only, and those who took the combination long-acting beta agonist with anti-inflammatory.
So this was a very reassuring study in terms of the safety of these medications.
But further to that, it also showed, in fact, that the benefits of the long-acting beta
agonist with the inhaled corticosteroid were equal, if not slightly superior, to the benefits
of the anti-inflammatory alone.
So a very productive study on both counts.
But it didn't look as if it was worth actually adding the LABA to it.
because there wasn't that much difference between the two.
You might as well just have the child on the steroid alone.
It's true.
And indeed, most children should only be treated with inhaled corticosteroids alone.
In fact, most children don't even need continuous anti-inflammatory medication.
So that's an important thing to say about this study.
It actually recruited children who had had a hospital admission
or severe asthma-related event requiring corticosteroids in the previous 12 months.
So we're already including a group of children who are at slightly higher risk of these events.
And indeed, those children are at the more severe end of the spectrum who might need continuous medication.
Most children in Australia don't need continuous anti-inflammatory medication for their asthma because they have mild intermittent episodes.
So earlier on in the year, there was a study in adults. What did that show? That was about 11,000 adults.
Exactly.
So these are very large studies because they are safety studies.
Most studies of medications in respiratory medicine, at least, and I think it's true
for most other disciplines, are looking for the benefits of a treatment.
And you don't need nearly as many people in a trial looking for benefits when you know
a drug is efficacious than you do in a trial where you're looking for much less frequent
events such as adverse events related to the potential danger of the drug. So these studies
had to be by nature very large and this was an 11,000 person study, a multi-centre study conducted
globally and what it showed too in adults was that the long-acting beta agonist combined with
the anti-inflammatory steroid was superior in efficacy and not inferior in safety in any respect.
So both in adults and children.
So when you say superior in efficacy,
the adult one showed that there was an added benefit
from adding the long-acting beta agonist.
Correct, in reducing the number of asthma episodes
requiring causes of oral corticosteroid.
Now, these were the Glaxo drugs.
There's two kind of competing drugs here.
There's Astra who produced one set of this combination
and there's Glaxo and they've been in fierce competition for years.
So Glaxo has funded these trials.
Is it going to apply to the Astra drug,
which is the one that a lot of GPs would be prescribing?
Well, that's a very good question.
In fact, these trials were mandated by the Food and Drug Authority in the US
to address this question of safety.
There has been what's called a black box, a black label warning
on the packaging of these medications in the US
and that has been because there were much earlier
some studies which were observational studies primarily
that suggested that long-acting beta agonists might be dangerous.
This is a problem in the US particularly
where people might take these two drugs in separate inhalers
and end up only taking the long-acting beta agonists.
The very point you made in your introduction is
that beta agonists alone as a maintenance treatment for asthma
are not safe and should not be taken without an anti-inflammatory.
But this is a situation that has happened in the US particularly
because medications are very expensive
and people often default to the treatment that works for them.
But you haven't answered my question about which is better,
the Astra preparation or the Glaxo one,
or can you apply what was found from the Glaxo study to the Astra medication?
Yes, apologies.
My long-winded preamble was to tell you that the FDA mandated
that all the manufacturers of these drugs conducted these studies.
So these are the Lacksaw-Smith-Kline studies.
And AstraZeneca has also published a study also this week in the New England Journal of Medicine
demonstrating in adults the safety of their preparation in exactly the same way in adults
and indeed showing that not only are they safe and not inferior to the anti-inflammatory alone,
they are superior in efficacy.
and the Novartis company, which also manufactures these drugs,
is still undertaking the tail end of their studies
and they will be published too.
So we will know across the board for this whole class of medications
from each of these studies.
Chris Jenkins, thanks for joining us.
Thanks very much, Norman.
Professor Christine Jenkins, Head of Respiratory Trials
at the George Institute in Sydney.
Last week, The Lancet published a paper from the UK
which on the face of it was quite disturbing
in terms of the 30-day death rates
in people starting anti-cancer treatment for breast and lung cancer.
According to cancer researcher Darren Saunders,
what may be more interesting than the paper is how the media reported it.
Darren works at the University of New South Wales.
Welcome to the Health Report, Darren.
Hi, Norman.
What did the study show?
The study is quite interesting, actually.
They took all of the data from the NHS for patients that had had treatment
for breast cancer or lung cancer in 2014, so it's almost 30,000 patients,
and they looked at mortality within a month of their last line of chemotherapy, basically,
and found that there were some factors that predetermined
which people would respond and which people would die
from those chemotherapies.
Now, that's not necessarily surprising.
The shock was how it was reported more than anything else.
And just briefly, what people were at most risk?
Was there any surprise?
Not really.
Things like age, people with lung cancer that were already smokers,
so people that were more frail tended not to respond as well
to chemotherapy, which is not that surprising.
And people obviously with palliative chemotherapy.
People with palliative did worse.
And there were some grainy differences between the different hospitals.
And there was differences between the hospitals which people should take note of.
So how was it reported?
The two main reports, one was in the Telegraph in the UK and one was in the Guardian,
and both got picked up on social media.
The Telegraph splashed with their sort of lead paragraph was all about chemotherapy
killing half the patients that get it.
Right.
And that's not anywhere in that paper does it say that.
And I've been through the press releases that went with it,
and nowhere in those press releases do they say that.
Okay, well, that's a good headline.
Yeah. And that got, as you can imagine, amplified massively on social media.
And I saw some really disturbing responses from patients and patients' families saying,
well, that's convinced me. I've told my doctor I don't want therapy.
Now, the study didn't compare how people went with or without therapy.
So, you know, people are making big decisions based on misreporting here.
And The Guardian?
The Guardian got it better. They actually pretty much covered the story well. It was less
sensationalist. But they made some important points, but they did it much better.
And the argument here, of course, is that because it goes out in social media, it washes against
our shores as well. So is there much evidence that it washed against our shores?
It did. It did. It was widely reported even by some science and health reporters within
Australia on social media, unfortunately.
Picking up on the Telegraph headline rather than the Guardian headline.
Yep, exactly. That was the headline that was quoted.
So it's literally viral. It's infectious.
Yeah, yeah. So it brings up this notion of, and forgive my language here, this notion of the unbearable asymmetry of bullshit, as Brian Earp, the philosopher in the UK, is called.
And that's this notion that the amount of energy necessary to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than it is to produce it in the first place.
How does this affect people like you who are cancer researchers?
Frustration is the first word I'd use. It's incredibly frustrating.
It's hard enough getting accurate information out to people in the first place.
and when it's, I wouldn't say deliberately misrepresented,
but obviously not well reported,
it gets most of us pretty upset actually, to be honest.
Well, what's the poor punter to do?
I mean, we had the catalyst on statins,
which reduced probably, you know,
some people would say cost 2,000 lives in Australia
over a period of time
because people at high risk went off the statins.
Yeah.
What is the poor punter to do
to actually work out what was a reliable article
versus non-reliable article?
It's really hard, especially when the byline is science editor of the Telegraph.
That should be coming from a reputable voice.
I guess I normally point patients towards the National Institutes of Health in America
or Cancer Research UK or the Cancer Institute in New South Wales
who have reputable, well-collated information.
So double-check before you decide that it's going to affect your therapy.
Definitely.
And this follows hard on the heels of bacon killing half the population.
That was a great example.
Pure meats and cancer.
Yeah, BBC reported that as being equally risky as asbestos and plutonium, which, you know, it's clearly not.
Yeah, but not, yeah.
Smells too good for that.
Darren, thanks for joining us.
Thanks, Norman.
Darren Saunders, who's in the Department of Pathology at the University of New South Wales
and gnashing his teeth over cancer research reporting.
And you're listening to the Health Report here on Radio National.
According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, depending on the state that you live in,
up to 50% of the population of Australia are functionally illiterate.
A proportion of these people will have dyslexia, but that's far from the only reason.
This Saturday, Learning Difficulties Australia's 2016 Eminent Researcher Award
is to be given to an old friend of the Health Report, Professor Marianne Wolfe,
who's Director of the Centre for Reading and Language Research at Tufts University in Boston,
and she's dragged herself into the studio. Welcome back, Marianne.
It's a pleasure to be back.
Of course, I have a multifactorial response to give you, and it's a developmental one.
So pardon me if I give you four different reasons at four different ages.
The first is zero to five.
We know that the gaps really begin before the children even walk in the kindergarten door.
So what we could do to enhance language development is so simple.
Literally reading to our children, speaking to our children every day, every night is one of the simplest antidote
to really the very grievous differences in language
in our privileged and underprivileged homes.
So this is the notorious word gap.
This is the notorious word gap in which 32 million less words are heard
by children who are between three and four who come from disadvantaged homes.
And it's not just quantitative, it's qualitative as well.
You know, the nature of the language that's being used.
But yes, so that's the first, the zero to five.
But if you've got 50% of the population, depending on, I think that's a Tasmanian figure, actually.
Yes, it is.
I think it's in other cities, in other states.
But if you've got a large proportion, even 30% is high, and they're parents, they're going to struggle to read to their children.
Absolutely.
There are wonderful things that we can do.
and part of it is due to the pediatricians
who are giving these various groups of children stories
that can be read either by the people who are the parents
or by librarians or by caretakers or by tape recorders.
This is the U.S. context.
This is the U.S. context.
It's called Reach Out and Read.
But any group can do this.
So there's all kinds of ways we can do that.
But actually I think the more pernicious factor is happening
between kindergarten and grade two and three.
And Norman, we have spoken about this before.
I see a certain recidivism going on in Australia
in our methods of teaching children.
So regardless of the gap...
So this is not the first time you've been to Australia.
This is definitely not the first time I've even spoken to you, Norman,
about things that will make people very upset.
And that is the nature of instruction that goes on to children
who come from whatever home they are.
So this is before we even get on to dyslexia.
Oh, well before.
And what you're talking about here is teachers training colleges, not teaching teachers evidence-based literacy.
Exactly.
I mean, what I really was, I was so hopeful about Australia, but I see a retreat to binary modes of instruction.
So what do you see happening?
I see instead of us really reflecting the research on evidence-based instruction and the work from...
I would say there are like 30 randomized controlled trials of this.
This is not.
Yes, this is nothing new.
I mean, well, there are new things.
And what we're talking about here, just to cut to the chase, is the evidence-based teaching is phonics.
Sounding out words, understanding the sounds within words and relating them to the written text, amongst other things.
Okay, amongst other things.
But the way that I want the whole public to understand this is that phonics provides the first scaffolding of a reading brain circuitry.
But by no means do people who have all the good intentions of the world in teaching whole language, we don't leave them behind.
We provide that scaffolding and expand it.
And for those of you people who are listening to this for the first time, whole language is the notion that there's something natural about reading.
Your point is that it's very unnatural.
Very unnatural.
We didn't evolve to read.
Yes.
And they think just by showing text and telling nice stories, kids will get it.
Yes.
And some kids will, but not all.
Right.
Between 50 and 60 percent, any method works.
But for the rest of our children, we are literally not giving them the lower rungs of the ladder.
So they will never, in fact, reach their potential as truly expert readers because of this.
So I'm used to hammering doctors for not being evidence-based.
Now we're hammering teachers.
What evidence have you got that there's recidivism amongst Australian teachers and they're contributing to this unacceptably high level of literacy?
What I have been doing for the last week, but also for the last several months, is really trying to understand from teachers, policymakers, administrators, what is going on.
And what seems to be is a regression to a kind of a binary way of thinking about instruction.
Binary?
Binary being phonics versus whole language.
And we can call it balanced, but it's not balanced.
And what we really need to do is to understand evidence-based gives us a scaffolding.
Now, it also helps all children who have various forms of impairments.
So dyslexia is between 5% and 10% of the population.
There are many other challenges, but if you give this scaffolding and then you expand it,
you see, the reading brain circuit is not simply about phonics.
That's the beginning.
I need teachers to realize they need to be explicit about everything over time.
So we're talking about rich semantic or vocabulary work.
So it's understanding the world and the context.
Exactly. Syntax, the grammar.
There's so much that's beautiful about this reading brain circuit that is literally being taught in one way or another versus a developmental sequenced way of bringing it all together.
So do you think primary school teachers understand that syntax and the grammar?
One of the really harsh realities is that primary teachers are given the responsibilities for all the ills that society is not addressing.
They were given 20, 25 or 30 children.
They were never trained to work with children with dyslexia or challenges.
And they are given usually one hour a week from someone outside
and no pull-out time for the children who need intensive work.
Now, we're going to run out of time very briefly.
Looking at the 5% of kids with dyslexia.
Five to 10, yes.
I've been on a campaign about this with teachers training colleges
and obviously failed miserably.
Yes.
Yes, I do with you.
All we can do is talk about it.
But talking about the 5% who've got dyslexia and really something neurological going on in their brain,
what's new there in terms of being able to help them?
One of the most exciting aspects of all this work in neuroscience
is that we understand that our previous conceptualization of dyslexia was all wrong.
It's not about a deficit or a defect.
It's about a difference in the brain organization that children,
The educational system has not understood that it's not the child, it's us.
We can learn to teach this by understanding how the reading brain circuit works and addressing each component.
That takes training, but we have evidence trials right now going on from NICHD.
We have wonderful methods that can, with intensive pull-out training, small group,
we can do so much good and release the potential of some of our most creative minds who are dyslexic.
So is handing an iPad to a baby changing the reading pathway?
Oh, goodness gracious.
The iPad is the new pacifier with the same problems.
But seriously, is the digital world changing?
The fourth factor, I would say, in functional illiteracy is the fact that the digital world is in fact changing attention,
especially in the young brain
which is very susceptible
so you have addiction problems
you have children who are literally developing
a reading brain circuit
that's short circuited
that doesn't have the advantages
because it's moving its attention
sometimes 27 times an hour
they're not developing concentration
so you're talking about video based material
with rapid intercutting
but there's so many aspects to the digital culture
that are changing us
but they're changing attention
memory, reliance on external platforms of knowledge
rather than building inside the children.
Now, most parents would think that they're giving their children,
we've only got a minute left,
these deeper knowledge and exposure to the world
through the digital environment.
What's a parent to do?
Well, a parent, first of all,
there's some wonderful work done by different people.
And what I would really suggest
is that we have a developmental model.
Under two, I want no iPads.
over to between two and five, very gradual.
At five to seven, I want only use of the digital work
in school for coding and programming.
And then over time, then we gradually use it ever gradually.
So it's not a tool for learning to read.
It is a tool that could be used carefully and critically.
Literally, we need scales of justice here, Norman.
And in one minute, I'm not going to be able to say this,
but I will say that what I hope is a biliterate brain
that is critically able to use and know when to use a digital reading
and when to use print at what developmental period.
So it's a biliterate brain over time, developmentally taught.
And Marianne Wolfe's got a couple of books coming out on that,
which we will no doubt promote when they do.
Marianne, thanks very much for joining us again on The Health Report.
Marianne Wolfe is Director of the Centre for Reading and Language Research
at Tufts University in Boston.
I'm Norman Swan, and you've been listening to The Health Report.
I do hope you can join us again next week.
